rw: Trading on material nonpublic information about a pending merger is illegal insider trading, because the executive profits from knowledge the public lacks, which undermines fair markets and violates securities law.

ww.Legal research work: Research uses public information and analysis; acting on a secret merger tip the public has not seen is not research work, so this label does not fit the executive's purchase.
ww.A stock split event: A stock split only changes the number of shares and their price, not company value; buying shares ahead of secret merger news is a different matter entirely.
ww.Normal diversification: Diversification means spreading money across many assets to reduce risk; buying one company's shares because of confidential merger news is a concentrated bet using illegal information, not diversification.

rw: FINRA is a self-regulatory organization, meaning the industry polices itself under SEC oversight, writing rules, licensing brokers, examining firms, and disciplining those who break the rules.

ww.A stock index covering the whole market: A stock index measures market performance, such as the S&P 500; FINRA does not track prices at all, it supervises brokerage firms and the people who work for them.
ww.A bank for investors who want to borrow: FINRA does not lend money to investors; it is a regulator that writes and enforces rules for brokers, and borrowing needs a bank or broker margin loan.
ww.A tax agency that collects taxes from al: Taxes are collected by the IRS, not FINRA; FINRA has no taxing power and instead oversees the conduct of broker-dealers and registered representatives in securities markets.

rw: SIPC protects customers when a brokerage fails and assets go missing, not when prices drop; a market-driven fall in value is investment risk the investor bears alone.

ww.Yes, up to the full value of all the sto: SIPC does not cover market losses, so full value is never guaranteed; it only restores missing cash and securities, up to $500,000 per customer, when a brokerage fails.
ww.Yes, it covers all losses, whether from: SIPC never covers losses from falling prices or bad investment choices; it responds only to a failed brokerage firm, so claiming it covers all losses is false.
ww.Yes, but only on weekends and public hol: SIPC has no weekend or holiday condition; its protection depends on the brokerage failing, not on the calendar, and still excludes losses caused by a market decline.

rw: A retiree needing steady income soon cannot afford large swings, so a conservative mix of bonds and stable assets protects principal while providing predictable interest and dividend income.

ww.Borrowing to buy more stocks on margin a: Margin means borrowing to buy more stocks, which magnifies losses; a retiree with little time to recover cannot safely take that kind of leveraged risk.
ww.All speculative penny stocks that may ga: Penny stocks are highly speculative and can lose most of their value quickly; a retiree needing steady income soon cannot rely on such unpredictable, risky holdings.
ww.Only options trading and futures trading: Options and futures are complex, leveraged instruments that can produce large losses and no regular income, so they suit speculation rather than a retiree's need for stability.

rw: Compound interest is earned on the original principal plus all interest already added, so each period's interest is larger than the last and growth accelerates over time.

ww.A fee on loans paid by borrowers to the: That describes a loan fee, meaning ordinary interest paid by a borrower to a lender; compound interest instead means interest also earns interest, which grows savings faster over time.
ww.A tax on interest earned on savings and: A tax on interest income is just a tax; compound interest is a growth mechanism for the balance itself, not a levy charged by the government.
ww.Interest earned only on the original amo: Interest earned only on the original amount is simple interest; compound interest differs precisely because past interest is added to the base and also earns interest.

rw: Year one gives $1,000 x 1.10 = $1,100, and year two gives $1,100 x 1.10 = $1,210, because the second year earns interest on interest.

ww.$1,100: $1,100 is only the value after one year ($1,000 x 1.10); a second year of growth is still needed, so it understates the two-year result.
ww.$2,000: $2,000 would require doubling in two years, which needs 100% growth; at 10% compounded, $1,000 reaches only $1,210, far short of that figure.
ww.$1,200: $1,200 treats growth as simple interest, adding $100 twice; compounding adds 10% of $1,100 in year two, which is $110, giving $1,210 instead.

rw: The Rule of 72 estimates doubling time as 72 divided by the annual rate, so 72 / 6 = 12 years for money growing at 6% a year.

ww.6 years: Six years comes from using the rate as the time; the Rule of 72 divides 72 by the rate, so 72 / 6 = 12 years, not 6.
ww.1 year: One year would require a 72% return, since 72 / 72 = 1; at 6% the formula gives 72 / 6 = 12 years instead.
ww.72 years: Seventy-two years confuses the numerator with the answer; the rule divides 72 by the 6% rate, which gives 12 years rather than the number 72 itself.

rw: Inflation risk is the chance that investment returns fail to outpace rising prices, so real purchasing power shrinks even when the account balance is growing in nominal terms.

ww.The chance a stock splits into two share: A stock split divides one share into several of lower price without changing total value; inflation risk concerns prices of goods rising faster than investment returns, which erodes purchasing power.
ww.The chance a bank closes its doors for g: A bank closing is institutional or credit risk, usually addressed by deposit insurance; inflation risk is about rising prices reducing what your money can buy over time.
ww.The chance of a tax audit by the revenue: An audit is a tax compliance event that has nothing to do with price levels; inflation risk is the loss of purchasing power when prices rise faster than returns.

rw: Rebalancing means selling assets that have grown too large and buying those that have shrunk, which returns the portfolio to its target allocation and keeps risk at the intended level.

ww.Selling everything and starting over in: Selling everything and moving to cash abandons the plan and may trigger taxes; rebalancing keeps the existing strategy and only restores the original mix of assets.
ww.Ignoring the portfolio for years on end: Ignoring a portfolio lets winners grow into an oversized share and shifts risk unnoticed; rebalancing is the opposite, an active periodic check that restores the intended weights.
ww.Buying only the best performer of the ye: Buying only the best performer concentrates risk and chases past returns; rebalancing usually trims winners and adds to laggards so the portfolio returns to its target allocation.

rw: The spread is the ask minus the bid, so $20.05 - $19.95 = $0.10, which is the cost a trader pays to buy and sell immediately.

ww.$20.00: $20.00 is roughly the midpoint of the bid and ask, not their difference; subtracting $19.95 from $20.05 gives a spread of only $0.10.
ww.$40.00: $40.00 comes from adding the bid and ask ($19.95 + $20.05); the spread requires subtraction, which gives $0.10, not the sum of the two quotes.
ww.$1.00: $1.00 is ten times too large; the ask of $20.05 minus the bid of $19.95 is only $0.10, a narrow spread typical of a liquid stock.

rw: The maturity date is when the bond ends and the issuer must repay the principal, called the face or par value, to the bondholder in full.

ww.The date interest is calculated each yea: Interest calculation or payment dates are separate from maturity; maturity is the final date when the issuer repays the face value, not a yearly interest date.
ww.The date the bond is rated by a rating a: Rating agencies assess a bond at issuance and afterward on their own schedule; that is unrelated to maturity, which is the date principal is repaid.
ww.The date the bond is first sold by the f: The first sale of a bond is its issue date; maturity comes at the end of the bond's life, when the issuer repays the face value.

rw: A credit rating is an independent assessment of how likely a borrower is to repay debt on time, with grades such as AAA down to D.

ww.A tax assessment made by the revenue age: Tax assessments are done by revenue agencies for property or income; a credit rating evaluates a borrower's capacity to repay debt, not what taxes are owed.
ww.A ranking of a stock's price from highes: Ranking stock prices from high to low is a price list; a credit rating measures a borrower's repayment ability and applies to debt issuers, not share prices.
ww.A list of dividends paid by a firm in th: A record of past dividends is a dividend history; credit ratings concern how reliably a borrower can pay interest and principal, not what a firm paid shareholders.

rw: Volatility measures the size and speed of price changes; a highly volatile asset swings sharply up and down, which means higher uncertainty and typically greater risk for holders.

ww.The total number of shares traded over a: Total shares traded in a day is trading volume; volatility measures how much and how quickly prices change, regardless of how many shares trade hands.
ww.The fees on a trade made through a broke: Trade fees are commissions or costs of transacting; volatility describes price movement of the asset itself, not what a broker or app charges to execute orders.
ww.The average price over a year for the st: An average price over a year is a mean price; volatility measures how far prices swing around that average, not the average value itself.

rw: The risk-return tradeoff says that to seek higher potential returns, investors generally must accept higher risk, including a greater chance of losing money along the way.

ww.Lower risk always gives higher returns t: Lower risk does not always bring higher returns; the tradeoff says the opposite, that safer investments usually offer lower expected returns than riskier ones over time.
ww.Risk and return are unrelated to each ot: Risk and return are closely linked; investors demand extra expected return for taking on added risk, so calling them unrelated contradicts a basic principle of investing.
ww.Higher returns always come with no risk: No investment gives higher returns with zero risk; the word always and the claim of no risk are false, since extra return compensates for taking on extra risk.

rw: Stocks have historically delivered the highest long-run returns among common asset classes but with the largest price swings, so they carry the greatest risk and reward together.

ww.Savings: Savings accounts offer stable, insured balances with low interest, so they carry low risk and low return, the opposite of the highest long-run risk and return.
ww.Cash only: Cash is the safest, most liquid asset with minimal return, so it has the lowest long-run risk and return rather than the highest.
ww.T-bills: Treasury bills are short-term government securities with very low default risk and modest yields, so they sit near the bottom of the risk and return scale.

rw: In an IPO, the underwriter, usually an investment bank, advises on price, buys or markets the shares, and sells them to investors, often taking on some risk.

ww.Audits the company only, and signs a rep: Auditing and signing off on financial statements is the job of an independent accountant; the underwriter instead helps price the offering and sells the new shares.
ww.Insures deposits at banks for the savers: Deposit insurance is provided by the FDIC for banks; an underwriter has no role in insuring savers and instead manages the sale of new securities.
ww.Sets tax rates for the firm and its owne: Tax rates are set by governments, not underwriters; an underwriter advises on offering price and distributes shares to investors in an IPO.

rw: NYSE stands for the New York Stock Exchange, one of the largest U.S. stock exchanges, where buyers and sellers trade shares of listed companies.

ww.A government agency that regulates tradi: The NYSE is a private marketplace, not a government agency; regulation of trading comes from the SEC, while the NYSE simply operates the exchange.
ww.A U.S. bank that lends money to firms an: Lending to firms and households is done by banks; the NYSE is a marketplace where shares trade and does not make loans.
ww.A credit bureau that reports on borrower: Credit bureaus such as Equifax track borrowers' debt histories; the NYSE is a stock exchange where listed company shares are bought and sold.

rw: Nasdaq is known for listing many technology and growth companies, including large names in software, semiconductors, and biotechnology, which gives it a strong tech identity.

ww.Only government bonds sold by the state: Government bonds are sold by the Treasury and states, not listed as a Nasdaq specialty; Nasdaq is an equity exchange known for technology and growth firms.
ww.Only utilities and power companies: Nasdaq lists companies across many industries, not just utilities; its best known listings are technology and growth firms, so the word only makes this option wrong.
ww.Only banks and lenders in the nation: Nasdaq lists companies from many sectors, and banks are only a small part; the exchange is mainly known for technology and growth firms rather than only lenders.

rw: The Dow Jones Industrial Average is a price-weighted index of 30 large U.S. companies, meaning higher-priced stocks have more influence on the index level than lower-priced ones.

ww.A bond index covering the whole bond mar: The Dow tracks 30 stocks, not bonds; a bond index would measure debt securities, while the Dow follows large U.S. company shares only.
ww.An index of small companies with prices: The Dow holds 30 large, established companies, not small ones; it is price-weighted, but small company indexes such as the Russell 2000 track smaller firms.
An index of 500 U.S. firms describes the S&P 500; the Dow has only 30 companies, so the count of firms does not match.

rw: The S&P 500 holds 500 large U.S. companies and weights each by market capitalization, so bigger firms influence the index more than smaller ones do.

ww.An index of 30 companies with prices add: An index of 30 firms using a divisor and price weighting describes the Dow, not the S&P 500, which has 500 stocks weighted by size.
ww.An index of bonds issued by large U.S. f: The S&P 500 contains stocks, not bonds; a bond index would track debt issued by corporations and governments, which is a different product.
ww.A government agency that rates the whole: The S&P 500 is a stock index, not an agency; it measures large company performance and does not rate or regulate anything in markets.

rw: Market capitalization equals shares outstanding times price per share, so 5,000,000 x $40 = $200,000,000, which is $200 million for the whole company.

ww.$125,000: $125,000 comes from dividing $5 million by $40, which is meaningless here; market cap multiplies shares by price, so 5,000,000 x $40 = $200 million.
ww.$20 million: $20 million would apply to a $4 share price (5 million x $4); at $40 the calculation of 5,000,000 x $40 gives $200 million.
ww.$8 million: $8 million would be 200,000 shares at $40 or 5 million shares at $1.60; with 5,000,000 shares at $40 the product is $200 million.

rw: A correction is a drop of 10% or more from a recent peak, smaller than a bear market, which is a decline of 20% or more.

ww.A tax change affecting investors and fir: A tax change is a policy event; a market correction describes price behavior, specifically a decline of at least 10% from a recent high.
ww.A rule change affecting the whole market: A rule change is regulatory; a correction refers to falling prices after a rise, not to any change in the rules governing the market.
ww.A 50% crash in stock prices over a week: A 50% crash in a week is far more extreme than a correction; a correction is a moderate decline of roughly 10% or more from a recent peak.

rw: The VIX is called the fear gauge because it rises when investors expect large market swings and buy protection, and it falls during calm, confident periods.

ww.The jobs index: The jobs index concerns employment data; the VIX instead measures expected stock market volatility, which is why it is known by a different nickname.
ww.The CPI index: The CPI measures consumer price inflation and is published by the government; the VIX tracks implied volatility in S&P 500 options and carries a different nickname.
ww.The dividend index: Dividends are cash payments from companies; the VIX does not measure dividends at all, since it reflects expected volatility from S&P 500 option prices.

rw: The bid-ask spread equals the ask minus the bid, so $25.10 - $24.90 = $0.20, which represents the transaction cost of trading in and out immediately.

ww.$0.10: $0.10 is half the real gap; the spread is the ask minus the bid, so $25.10 - $24.90 = $0.20, not $0.10.
ww.$25.00: $25.00 is near the midpoint of the two quotes, not their difference; subtracting the bid from the ask yields $0.20 instead.
ww.$50.00: $50.00 adds the bid and ask ($24.90 + $25.10); the spread is a difference, so the correct calculation is $25.10 - $24.90 = $0.20.

rw: When the price touches the $54 stop, the stop order becomes a market order and sells at the next available price, which may differ slightly from $54.

ww.The stock is delisted from the exchange: A stop-loss triggers a sale order, not a delisting; delisting is an exchange decision about a company and has nothing to do with the investor's order.
ww.Nothing happens to the stock until the p: The order is triggered when the price falls to $54, so something does happen; waiting for a price rise would defeat the purpose of a stop-loss.
ww.You buy more shares at the lower price a: A stop-loss is a sell order, not a buy order; it exits the position to limit losses rather than adding shares at the lower price.

rw: A day order is valid only for the current trading session and expires at the end of the trading day if it has not been filled.

ww.An order that lasts for a whole week if: A day order lasts only until the market closes on the day it is placed, not a week; longer-lasting instructions are called good-til-canceled orders.
ww.An order that never expires and stays op: An order that stays open until the investor cancels it is a good-til-canceled order, not a day order, which expires automatically at the close.
ww.An order that lasts for a whole year if: A day order does not last a year; it ends at the close of that trading day if unfilled, so a year-long duration is incorrect.

rw: A short seller profits when the price falls: ($50 - $42) x 100 shares = $8 x 100 = $800, ignoring costs.

ww.$5,000: $5,000 would be the dollar value of 100 shares at $50, not the profit; profit equals the price drop per share ($8) times 100 shares.
ww.$80: $80 uses the $8 drop but forgets to multiply by 100 shares; the correct profit is $8 x 100 = $800.
ww.$4,200: $4,200 is the cost to buy back the 100 shares at $42; profit is the difference between the sale and buyback, ($50 - $42) x 100 = $800.

rw: A circuit breaker temporarily halts trading after a large decline, such as a 7% drop in the S&P 500, to calm panic selling and let investors reassess.

ww.A tax on trades made by day traders and: Circuit breakers are not taxes; they are exchange rules that pause trading when prices fall sharply, giving investors time to absorb information and avoid panic.
ww.An electrical switch that cuts power to: Though the name sounds electrical, a market circuit breaker is not a power switch; it is a trading rule that triggers halts after sharp declines.
ww.A type of order placed by a broker for a: Order types, such as limit or stop orders, are instructions from clients; a circuit breaker is a market-wide rule, not an order a broker places.

rw: High-frequency trading uses powerful computers and fast algorithms to place a very large number of orders in fractions of a second, often profiting from tiny price differences.

ww.Trading only once a year on a set date b: High-frequency trading is the opposite of rare trading; trading once a year would be extremely low frequency, while these firms trade thousands of times each second.
ww.Trading by mail between firms and invest: High-frequency trading is electronic and measured in milliseconds or microseconds; trading by mail is far too slow to match that description.
ww.Trading by phone only between clerks on: Phone trading by floor clerks is a slow, manual method; high-frequency trading depends on automated algorithms and fast connections rather than human voices.

rw: A 3-for-1 split triples the share count and divides the price by 3, so $120 / 3 = $40, leaving total company value unchanged.

ww.$360: $360 multiplies the price by 3, but a 3-for-1 split divides the price by 3; $120 / 3 = $40 per share.
ww.$117: $117 subtracts 3 from the price, which is not how a split works; the price is divided by the split ratio, so $120 / 3 = $40.
ww.$123: $123 adds 3 to the price, which has no basis in a split; dividing $120 by the ratio of 3 gives about $40 per share.

rw: A 2-for-1 split doubles the number of shares, so 50 shares x 2 = 100 shares, while the price per share is cut in half.

ww.50 shares: Staying at 50 shares would mean no split occurred; a 2-for-1 split doubles holdings to 100 shares, with the price halving so total value stays the same.
ww.25 shares: Dividing 50 by 2 gives 25, which would describe a reverse split; in a 2-for-1 forward split the share count doubles to 100.
ww.52 shares: Adding 2 shares to get 52 misreads the ratio; a 2-for-1 split multiplies shares by 2, so 50 shares become 100 shares.

rw: A reverse split reduces the number of shares outstanding and raises the price per share proportionally, such as 1-for-10, leaving total company value unchanged.

ww.A merger of two firms into one larger co: A merger combines two firms into one; a reverse split changes the share count of a single company and does not combine businesses or swap shares between firms.
ww.A dividend paid out of profits to each h: A dividend distributes profit to shareholders as cash or stock; a reverse split does not pay anything, it only changes the share count and price.
ww.A company increases its share count and: Increasing the share count while lowering the price describes a forward stock split; a reverse split does the opposite by cutting shares and raising price.

rw: The SEC is the federal agency that regulates securities markets, enforces securities laws, and protects investors by requiring companies and professionals to disclose accurate information.

ww.A credit bureau that collects and report: A credit bureau compiles consumer credit histories; the SEC regulates securities markets, enforces disclosure rules, and protects investors, which is a different mission altogether.
ww.A stock exchange where investors buy and: A stock exchange, such as the NYSE, is a marketplace for trading shares; the SEC is a regulator that oversees exchanges rather than operating one.
ww.A private bank that lends money to compa: The SEC is a government regulator, not a private bank, and it does not lend money; its role is overseeing markets and enforcing securities laws.

rw: SIPC is the Securities Investor Protection Corporation, which helps return customers' cash and securities, up to $500,000, when a member brokerage fails or assets go missing.

ww.A tax agency that collects taxes on inve: Taxes on investment gains are collected by the IRS; SIPC is a nonprofit that protects customers' assets if a brokerage firm fails.
ww.A bank insurer that protects deposits wh: Bank deposits are insured by the FDIC; SIPC is separate and covers securities and cash at failed brokerage firms, not at commercial banks.
ww.A stock index that follows the price of: A stock index tracks prices of selected companies; SIPC is not an index, it is a protection organization for customers of failed brokerage firms.

rw: SIPC protects against missing assets when a brokerage fails but never against falling prices; market losses are an ordinary investment risk the investor must bear.

ww.Yes, all losses are covered by the fund: SIPC does not cover losses in all cases; it excludes declines in market value, and it only helps when a brokerage fails and assets are missing.
ww.Yes, but only for bonds and not for stoc: SIPC covers stocks, bonds, and mutual funds held at a failed brokerage, so limiting it to bonds is wrong; it also does not cover market declines.
ww.Yes, up to $1 million always, whatever t: SIPC limits are $500,000 per customer, including $250,000 for cash, not $1 million, and the protection never applies to losses from price declines of any cause.

rw: The Securities Act of 1933 requires companies to register new securities and give investors accurate disclosure when shares are first sold to the public in the primary market.

ww.Insuring deposits at banks and credit un: Deposit insurance came from the Banking Act of 1933 and later the FDIC; the Securities Act of 1933 is about disclosure when securities are first sold.
ww.Regulating trading on exchanges and the: Regulating exchange trading and broker conduct is the job of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934; the 1933 Act focuses on new issues.
ww.Setting tax rates for individuals and co: Tax rates are set by tax legislation, such as the Internal Revenue Code; the Securities Act of 1933 addresses securities registration and disclosure instead.

rw: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 regulates trading of existing securities in the secondary market and created the SEC to enforce those rules.

ww.Setting minimum wage rates for workers i: Minimum wage is covered by labor law such as the Fair Labor Standards Act; the 1934 Act concerns securities trading and created the SEC.
ww.Regulating new issues only, when first s: Regulating new issues when first sold describes the Securities Act of 1933; the 1934 Act covers trading after issuance and created the SEC.
ww.Insuring deposits at banks and credit un: Bank deposit insurance is handled by the FDIC, created in 1933; the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 governs securities trading, not deposits.

rw: Sarbanes-Oxley followed scandals such as Enron and WorldCom, and it targeted corporate accounting fraud by requiring accurate financial reporting, stronger internal controls, and executive accountability.

ww.Bank deposits and savings accounts in th: Bank deposits are covered by banking laws and the FDIC; Sarbanes-Oxley focuses on public company accounting and financial reporting, not savings accounts.
ww.Import duties on goods coming from other: Import duties are tariffs set by trade policy; Sarbanes-Oxley deals with corporate governance and financial reporting at public companies, not trade taxes.
ww.Consumer loans from banks and credit car: Consumer lending is regulated by laws on credit and banking; Sarbanes-Oxley addresses accounting fraud and reporting at public companies instead.

rw: Dodd-Frank, enacted in 2010, responded to the 2008 financial crisis by adding oversight of banks and markets, creating the CFPB, and imposing new rules on derivatives.

ww.The Great Depression of the 1930s in the: The Great Depression led to the 1933 and 1934 securities acts; Dodd-Frank came much later, in 2010, in response to a more recent crisis.
ww.The dot-com bubble of the late 1990s in: The dot-com bubble of the late 1990s helped lead to reforms around 2002 such as Sarbanes-Oxley, not to the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010.
ww.A tax dispute between a firm and the rev: Dodd-Frank is broad financial legislation, not a response to a tax dispute; it addressed systemic risk and consumer protection after the 2008 crisis.

rw: The P/E ratio equals share price divided by earnings per share, showing how many dollars investors pay for each dollar of annual earnings.

ww.Debt divided by equity for the whole fir: Debt divided by equity is the debt-to-equity ratio, a measure of leverage; the P/E ratio instead compares a stock's price with its earnings per share.
ww.Earnings divided by share price, the inv: Earnings divided by share price is the earnings yield, which is the inverse of P/E; P/E itself puts the price in the numerator.
ww.Dividends divided by price per share hel: Dividends divided by price is the dividend yield; the P/E ratio uses earnings per share, not dividends, in the denominator against share price.

rw: P/E equals price divided by earnings per share, so $60 / $4 = 15, meaning investors pay $15 for each $1 of annual earnings.

ww.56: 56 comes from subtracting $4 from $60; the P/E ratio divides price by earnings per share, giving $60 / $4 = 15 instead.
ww.240: 240 results from multiplying $60 by $4; P/E requires division, so $60 / $4 = 15, not the product of the two numbers.
ww.0.067: 0.067 is the earnings yield, $4 / $60, which is the inverse; P/E divides price by earnings, giving $60 / $4 = 15.

rw: EPS equals net income divided by shares outstanding, so $2,000,000 / 500,000 = $4.00 earned per share.

ww.$40: $40 would result from an arithmetic slip, such as treating $20 million as net income; with $2 million and 500,000 shares, EPS is $4.00.
ww.$0.25: $0.25 is the inverse, 500,000 / $2,000,000; EPS divides income by shares, so $2,000,000 / 500,000 = $4.00, not a quarter dollar.
ww.$1,000: $1,000 is far too high; dividing $2 million by 500,000 shares gives $4.00, since $2,000,000 / 500,000 = 4.

rw: Dividend yield equals annual dividend divided by price, so $2 / $50 = 0.04, or 4%, the cash return from dividends alone.

ww.25%: 25% comes from inverting the fraction, $50 / $2 = 25; dividend yield is dividend divided by price, so $2 / $50 = 4%.
ww.2%: 2% would require a $1 dividend on a $50 stock; with a $2 dividend the calculation is $2 / $50 = 4%.
ww.$100: $100 multiplies the dividend by the price ($2 x $50); yield is a percentage found by dividing $2 by $50, which gives 4%, not a dollar amount.

rw: The payout ratio equals dividends divided by earnings, showing what share of profit goes to shareholders and how much the company retains for growth.

ww.Profit divided by revenue for the year: Profit divided by revenue is the net profit margin, which measures profitability; the payout ratio measures how much of earnings is distributed as dividends.
ww.Debt divided by assets owned by the firm: Debt divided by assets is a leverage measure called the debt ratio; the payout ratio concerns dividends relative to earnings, not borrowing.
ww.Price divided by earnings per share held: Price divided by earnings per share is the P/E ratio, a valuation measure; the payout ratio compares dividends paid with net earnings instead.

rw: Payout ratio equals dividends divided by earnings, so $2 / $5 = 0.40, or 40%, meaning the company pays out two-fifths of earnings.

ww.7%: 7% results from an unrelated calculation; the payout ratio divides the $2 dividend by $5 of earnings per share, which gives 40%.
ww.60%: 60% is the retention ratio, the share of earnings kept, which is $3 / $5; the payout ratio is $2 / $5 = 40%.
ww.250%: 250% inverts the fraction, $5 / $2 = 2.5; the payout ratio divides dividends by earnings, so $2 / $5 = 40%.

rw: Price-to-book compares market price per share with book value per share, showing how much investors pay relative to the company's net assets on its books.

ww.Price to sales for the whole firm in the: Price to sales compares price with revenue per share; price-to-book compares market price per share with the book value per share on the balance sheet.
ww.Price to dividend for the whole firm eac: Price to dividend relates to yield and is not price-to-book; the P/B ratio uses book value, meaning assets minus liabilities, per share.
ww.Debt to equity for the whole firm in the: Debt to equity measures leverage; price-to-book is a valuation ratio that compares a stock's market price with the accounting value of equity per share.

rw: ROE equals net income divided by shareholders' equity, showing how much profit a company generates from the money its owners have invested.

ww.Revenue divided by equity for the year: Revenue divided by equity is not a standard profitability measure; ROE uses net income in the numerator, not sales, to measure profit earned on equity.
ww.Net income divided by sales, the profit: Net income divided by sales is the profit margin; ROE divides net income by shareholders' equity, so the denominator makes the difference.
ww.Equity divided by assets for the whole f: Equity divided by assets is the equity ratio, which shows financing structure; ROE measures profit relative to equity, with net income on top.

rw: ROE equals net income divided by shareholders' equity, so $3 million / $20 million = 0.15, or 15%.

ww.6.7%: 6.7% results from inverting or misreading the numbers; ROE is net income divided by equity, so $3 million / $20 million = 15%.
ww.23%: 23% does not follow from the data; dividing $3 million by $20 million gives 0.15, which is 15%, not 23%.
ww.60%: 60% is far too high; ROE is $3 million / $20 million = 0.15, so only 15 cents of profit per dollar of equity.

rw: The current ratio equals current assets divided by current liabilities, so $600,000 / $400,000 = 1.5, meaning $1.50 of liquid assets for each $1 owed.

ww.100,000: 100,000 matches no valid calculation here; the current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities, so $600,000 / $400,000 = 1.5, which is a ratio rather than a dollar figure.
ww.0.67: 0.67 inverts the ratio ($400,000 / $600,000); the current ratio puts current assets on top, so $600,000 / $400,000 = 1.5.
ww.200,000: 200,000 is the dollar difference ($600,000 - $400,000), known as working capital; the current ratio divides instead of subtracting, so $600,000 / $400,000 = 1.5.

rw: Intrinsic value is the estimated true worth of an asset, found by analyzing fundamentals such as earnings, cash flows, and growth, regardless of the quoted market price.

ww.The IPO price paid by the first buyers o: An IPO price is what first buyers paid, set by supply and demand at issue; intrinsic value is an estimate of true worth from fundamentals.
ww.The current market price on the day it i: The current market price is what investors pay now; intrinsic value is a separate estimate of what the asset is truly worth, which may differ.
ww.The par value printed on the face of the: Par value is a nominal legal figure printed on a certificate and often unrelated to worth; intrinsic value is based on fundamentals, not a printed number.

rw: Support is a price level where falling prices tend to stop, and resistance is a level where rising prices tend to stall, both used in technical analysis.

ww.Tax brackets for income earned by worker: Tax brackets are income tax bands for workers; support and resistance are price levels on a chart, so this option confuses taxation with technical analysis.
ww.Dividend dates set by the board of direc: Dividend dates are corporate calendar events; support and resistance refer to prices where buying or selling pressure has tended to halt a trend.
ww.Interest rates charged by banks on loans: Interest rates charged on loans are credit pricing; support and resistance describe price behavior on a chart, not borrowing costs from banks.

rw: Beta measures a stock's volatility relative to the market; a beta above 1 means it swings more than the market, and below 1 means less.

ww.A profit margin shown on the income stat: A profit margin is an income statement ratio; beta is a market-risk measure comparing a stock's price movement with the overall market.
ww.A credit rating given to a firm by a rat: A credit rating gauges borrowers' repayment ability; beta instead measures how sensitive a stock's returns are to market movements.
ww.A dividend measure used by analysts to r: Beta is not a dividend measure; it compares a stock's price swings with the market, while dividend measures such as yield or payout ratio concern income.

rw: Expected move equals beta times the market move, so 1.5 x 10% = 15%, meaning the stock is expected to rise more than the market.

ww.6.7%: 6.7% results from dividing 10% by 1.5; beta multiplies the market move, so 1.5 x 10% = 15%, not a division.
ww.10%: A 10% rise would fit a beta of 1.0; with a beta of 1.5 the stock amplifies the market's move to about 15%.
ww.1.5%: 1.5% mistakes the beta for a percentage; multiplying the beta of 1.5 by the market's 10% rise gives 15%.

rw: Expected move equals beta times the market move, so 0.5 x 8% = 4%; a low-beta stock falls only half as much as the market.

ww.12%: 12% would result from 1.5 x 8%, a beta of 1.5; with a beta of 0.5 the stock moves only half of the market's 8%.
ww.8%: An 8% fall would fit a beta of 1.0; a beta of 0.5 means the stock is expected to fall by half the market's decline, which is 4%.
ww.16%: 16% would result from a beta of 2.0 (2 x 8%); the given beta of 0.5 halves the move, giving 0.5 x 8% = 4%.

rw: Alpha is the return earned above what the market and the investment's risk would predict, so a positive alpha suggests the manager added value beyond market exposure.

ww.Market volatility, which shows how much: Volatility describes price swings, and the measure relative to the market is beta; alpha is excess return after adjusting for risk, not a measure of daily swings.
ww.A dividend that a company pays to its sh: A quarterly payment to shareholders is a dividend; alpha is a performance measure for excess return and has nothing to do with company payouts.
ww.A tax that investors pay on the profit t: A tax on profit from selling shares is capital gains tax; alpha is a measure of risk-adjusted excess return, not a tax paid by investors.

rw: The Sharpe ratio measures risk-adjusted return, dividing excess return over the risk-free rate by standard deviation, so higher values show more return per unit of risk.

ww.Trading volume levels: Trading volume counts shares traded and is unrelated to the Sharpe ratio, which compares a portfolio's excess return with the risk it took on.
ww.Debt level of a firm: Debt level of a firm is measured by leverage ratios such as debt-to-equity; the Sharpe ratio evaluates investment performance relative to its risk.
ww.Dividend yield rates: Dividend yield is annual dividends divided by price; the Sharpe ratio instead evaluates how much return an investment delivers for each unit of risk taken.

rw: The efficient market hypothesis states that prices already reflect all available information, so it is very difficult to consistently beat the market using known facts.

ww.The idea that prices never change from y: The hypothesis does not say prices never change; prices move constantly as new information arrives, and it claims they already reflect what is publicly known.
ww.The idea that only insiders can ever mak: The hypothesis says information is quickly reflected in prices for everyone, so insiders are not the only ones who can profit, and it claims no one beats the market consistently.
ww.The idea that markets are always wrong s: The hypothesis does not say markets are always wrong; it says prices are generally fair, which makes it hard for investors to win easily.

rw: Portfolio rebalancing means adjusting holdings back to target allocations, usually by selling assets that have grown too large and buying those that have fallen behind.

ww.Ignoring the performance of every holdin: Ignoring holdings would let allocations drift unchecked; rebalancing requires reviewing performance and restoring the target mix, so it is an active step.
ww.Buying only one stock and holding it for: Holding one stock for years concentrates risk and is the opposite of rebalancing, which maintains a diversified mix of assets in set proportions.
ww.Selling everything in the account at onc: Selling the whole account at once ends the investment plan and may create taxes; rebalancing only trims and adds enough to restore the original proportions.

rw: The portfolio is now 70% stocks instead of 60%, so selling some stocks and buying bonds brings it back to the 60/40 target.

ww.Buy more stocks to push it further: Buying more stocks would push the portfolio even further from 60/40, increasing risk; rebalancing requires moving back toward the target mix, not away from it.
ww.Do nothing and just wait for it: Doing nothing leaves the allocation at 70/30, with more risk than intended; rebalancing is an active step that restores the 60/40 target.
ww.Sell bonds only and buy none: Selling bonds only and buying none would reduce the bond share below the 30% it already has, moving even further from the 40% target.

rw: Stocks have historically earned higher long-term returns than bonds or cash, but they also swing more in price, so they combine higher return with greater volatility.

ww.Cash: Cash is stable but earns little, often less than inflation, so it has low volatility and low returns, the reverse of higher returns with more volatility.
ww.T-bills: Treasury bills are safe, short-term, low-yield securities with minimal price swings, so they do not offer high long-term returns with high volatility.
ww.Savings: Savings accounts offer stable balances with low interest, so they have both low returns and low volatility, unlike stocks, which pair higher returns with larger swings.

rw: Time horizon is the length of time an investor expects to hold an investment before needing the money, and it guides how much risk is appropriate.

ww.The tax year, which is the twelve months: The tax year is a reporting period for filing returns and has nothing to do with investing goals; time horizon is how long money will be invested.
ww.The market's hours, which are the times: Market hours are the trading times of an exchange; time horizon refers to an investor's own holding period, not when trades can be made.
ww.The stock's age, which is the number of: A stock's age is the number of years since a company was founded; time horizon concerns the investor's plan, not the history of the company.

rw: With 40 years until retirement, a young saver has time to recover from downturns, so holding more equities for higher expected growth is typically appropriate.

ww.No risk at all in any of their assets or: No investor can eliminate all risk and still earn meaningful returns; a 25-year-old with 40 years to invest can actually accept more risk, not zero.
ww.Only short-term loans and bills from ban: Short-term loans and bills offer low returns that may lag inflation over 40 years, so limiting a young investor to them wastes the long time horizon.
ww.Only cash held in a bank account at the: Cash in a bank account is safe but earns little and may not keep up with inflation, which is costly over a 40-year horizon.

rw: Needing money next year calls for stable assets that can be sold quickly at predictable prices, so mostly stable, liquid holdings suit a retiree.

ww.All aggressive growth stocks: Aggressive growth stocks can fall sharply, and a retiree needing money next year would have little time to recover, so all-aggressive holdings are unsuitable.
ww.Illiquid land and houses: Land and houses are illiquid and can take months to sell, so they are a poor fit for someone needing cash within a year.
ww.Only speculative options: Speculative options can expire worthless, wiping out the entire investment, which is a poor choice for a retiree who needs funds next year.

rw: Yield to maturity is the total annualized return on a bond if held until it matures, counting coupons, any price gain or loss, and reinvestment of interest.

ww.The tax rate on bond interest paid to ho: A tax rate on bond interest concerns taxation; yield to maturity measures the bond's total expected annual return when held until maturity, not what is owed.
ww.The coupon rate only, the yearly interes: The coupon rate alone is only the annual interest on face value; yield to maturity also reflects the price paid and the gain or loss at maturity.
ww.The stock dividend paid each year to hol: A stock dividend is a payment on equity; yield to maturity applies to bonds and measures total return from interest and price change to maturity.

rw: Annual interest equals the coupon rate times face value, so 6% x $1,000 = $60 per year, usually paid in two $30 installments.

ww.$6: $6 would be 0.6% of $1,000; a 6% coupon pays 6% x $1,000 = $60 per year, so $6 is ten times too small.
ww.$600: $600 would be a 60% coupon; the correct calculation is 6% x $1,000 = $60, so $600 is ten times too large.
ww.$1,060: $1,060 is the face value plus one year's interest, which is what the holder gets at maturity in the final year, not the annual interest alone.

rw: Face or par value is the amount the issuer repays at maturity, and it is also the base on which the coupon interest is calculated.

ww.The market price of the bond: The market price is what the bond currently trades for and can differ from par; face value is the fixed amount repaid at maturity.
ww.The broker fee charged on it: A broker fee is a transaction cost and is unrelated to the bond's face value, which is the principal that the issuer returns at maturity.
ww.The annual interest paid on it: The annual interest payment is the coupon, computed as coupon rate times face value; it is not itself the face value that is repaid at maturity.

rw: A bond trades at a discount when its market price is below its face value, so a buyer pays less than the amount repaid at maturity.

ww.Its price is above face value: A price above face value is a premium, not a discount; a discount bond trades below face value, usually because yields have risen since issue.
ww.It has defaulted on debts: Trading at a discount does not mean default; many healthy bonds trade below par when market rates rise above their coupon rates.
ww.It is given away free of charge: A discount describes a lower market price, not a giveaway; buyers still pay money, and they receive the face value at maturity plus interest.

rw: A lower credit rating signals higher default risk, meaning investors face a greater chance the issuer will fail to pay interest or principal, so they demand higher yields.

ww.No risk involved: Every bond carries some risk, and a lower rating signals more risk, not none; no risk involved contradicts what ratings are designed to show.
ww.Guaranteed repayment: No rating guarantees repayment; a lower rating suggests a higher chance of default, so claiming guaranteed repayment is the reverse of what the signal means.
ww.Lower default risk: Lower default risk would be indicated by a higher rating such as AAA; a lower rating suggests the opposite, a greater chance of default.

rw: Junk bonds, also called high-yield bonds, are rated below investment grade, so they pay higher yields to compensate for a greater chance the issuer defaults.

ww.Government bonds that are backed by the: Government bonds backed by full faith are the safest category, such as Treasuries, and are not junk; junk bonds are rated below investment grade.
ww.Insured bonds that guarantee the investo: Junk bonds are not insured or guaranteed; they carry high default risk, which is why issuers must offer higher yields to attract buyers.
ww.Zero-risk bonds that pay a high rate wit: No bond is zero-risk with a high rate; junk bonds pay more precisely because investors can lose money if the issuer defaults.

rw: Duration measures a bond's price sensitivity to interest rate changes; a longer duration means the price falls more when rates rise and rises more when rates fall.

ww.The credit rating of the issuer of the b: The issuer's credit rating measures default risk, not duration; duration instead measures how much a bond's price changes when interest rates move.
ww.The issuer's age in years since the firm: An issuer's age has no bearing on duration, which is a calculation based on a bond's cash flows and timing, not on how old the firm is.
ww.The coupon payment made to the holder ea: The coupon payment is annual interest on face value; duration is a different measure of how sensitive a bond's price is to rate changes.

rw: A Treasury bill is a short-term U.S. government debt security, maturing in a year or less, sold at a discount and redeemed at face value.

ww.A mutual fund holding many bonds and not: A fund that holds many bonds is a bond mutual fund; a Treasury bill is a single short-term government debt security, not a pooled fund.
ww.A stock issued by a firm and traded on m: A stock represents ownership in a company; a Treasury bill is debt issued by the U.S. government, so it pays no dividends and trades differently.
ww.A long-term corporate bond that pays int: A Treasury bill matures in one year or less and pays no coupons, so it is not a long-term corporate bond paying interest twice a year.

rw: Municipal bonds are issued by states and local governments to fund public projects, and their interest is often exempt from federal income tax, which makes them attractive to high earners.

ww.Bonds issued by corporations to raise mo: Corporate bonds come from companies; municipal bonds are issued by states, cities, and local governments to finance public projects, so this option names the wrong issuer.
ww.Stocks of cities that pay dividends to t: Municipal bonds are debt, not stocks; cities do not issue shares and the holders receive interest, not dividends, so this describes no real product.
ww.Bonds issued by the federal government,: Federal government bonds are Treasuries, which are exempt from state tax; municipal bonds come from states and localities and often have tax-exempt interest.

rw: A call provision gives the issuer the right to redeem the bond before maturity, often when interest rates have fallen, so the issuer can refinance more cheaply.

ww.A voting right held by common stockholde: Voting rights belong to common stockholders and are unrelated to bonds; a call provision lets the bond issuer redeem the bond early.
ww.The investor's right to sell the bond ba: The investor's right to sell the bond back to the issuer is a put provision; a call provision gives that right to the issuer.
ww.A dividend right held by preferred share: Dividend rights for preferred shareholders concern stock, not bonds; a call provision is a bond feature that lets the issuer repay early.

rw: Common shareholders typically vote on directors and major corporate matters and hold a residual claim on assets after creditors and preferred holders are paid.

ww.No rights at all in the firm or in its a: Common shareholders are owners with rights such as voting and a residual claim, so saying they have no rights at all is false.
ww.Guaranteed dividends every quarter, win: Dividends are never guaranteed for common stock; the board decides whether to pay them, and they can be cut in a poor year.
ww.Fixed interest paid each year to holders: Fixed interest payments are a feature of bonds; common shareholders instead receive variable dividends, if any, and share in residual assets.

rw: In liquidation, creditors, including bondholders, must be paid before shareholders, because debt holders have a legal claim while shareholders hold only a residual claim.

ww.Employees' bonuses paid out before other: Bonuses are not senior claims; in liquidation, secured creditors and other creditors are paid before shareholders, and ordinary bonuses do not outrank them.
ww.The CEO and other top managers of the fi: Managers have no special priority in liquidation; unpaid wages aside, payment order starts with creditors and ends with shareholders, not with top executives.
ww.Common shareholders before any of the ot: Common shareholders come last in liquidation, after creditors and preferred holders, so they cannot be paid ahead of the other creditors.

rw: The call has no value at $48 because it is below the $50 strike, so the buyer loses only the $3 premium paid, per share.

ww.$0: $0 would be correct only if the premium were free; the buyer paid $3 and the option expires worthless since $48 is below the $50 strike.
ww.$2: $2 is the gap between the strike and stock price ($50 - $48), but the call is out of the money and worthless, so the loss is the whole premium.
ww.$50: $50 is the strike price, not the loss; a call buyer's maximum loss is limited to the premium paid, which is $3 per share.

rw: The call pays $48 - $40 = $8 at expiration, and subtracting the $2 premium paid gives a net profit of $6 per share.

ww.$10: $10 ignores the premium and overstates the gain; the payoff is $48 - $40 = $8, then subtract the $2 premium, which leaves $6.
ww.$8: $8 is the intrinsic value ($48 - $40) before subtracting the $2 premium paid; profit is the payoff minus the cost, which gives $6.
ww.$2: $2 is only the premium paid, which is the cost, not the profit; the option is worth $8 at expiration, so net profit is $8 - $2 = $6.

rw: Hedging means taking an offsetting position, such as buying a put against a stock holding, to reduce the risk of another investment or exposure.

ww.Ignoring risk and hoping for the best ou: Ignoring risk is the opposite of hedging; hedging is a deliberate step to protect against losses, not a hope for a good outcome.
ww.Increasing risk to chase higher returns: Increasing risk to chase returns is speculation or leverage; hedging aims to reduce risk, even if it limits some of the potential gain.
ww.Day trading for small gains several time: Day trading means frequent buying and selling for small gains, which is speculation; hedging is a protective strategy that offsets risk elsewhere.

rw: A REIT is a real estate investment trust that owns or finances income-producing property and must distribute most of its income to shareholders, offering real estate exposure without buying buildings.

ww.A bank account that is insured and earns: An insured account that earns a small return describes a savings account or certificate; a REIT is a company that owns property and trades like a stock.
ww.A credit card that gives rewards on trav: A rewards credit card is a payment product; a REIT is an investment vehicle that owns or finances real estate and passes income to investors.
ww.A type of bond that pays a fixed rate of: A REIT is not a bond with a fixed rate; it is a real estate company that distributes most of its income as dividends to shareholders.

rw: NAV equals total assets minus liabilities, divided by shares outstanding, giving the per-share value of a fund, usually calculated at the end of each trading day.

ww.A fund's fees and costs charged each yea: Fees and costs charged to holders are the fund's expense ratio; NAV is the per-share value of the fund's net assets, not its costs.
ww.A stock's market price on the day it is: A stock's market price is set by trading, whereas NAV is calculated from the value of a fund's holdings less its liabilities, per share.
ww.A bond's coupon rate paid to holders eac: A bond's coupon rate is its stated interest; NAV applies to funds and measures net assets per share, so it has no link to coupons.

rw: NAV equals assets minus liabilities divided by shares, so ($90 million - $10 million) / 4 million = $80 million / 4 million = $20 per share.

ww.$25: $25 would result from dividing $100 million by 4 million; NAV subtracts liabilities first, so ($90 million - $10 million) / 4 million = $20.
ww.$320: $320 results from multiplying $80 million by 4 rather than dividing; NAV divides net assets by shares, so $80 million / 4 million = $20.
ww.$22.50: $22.50 ignores the liabilities; dividing the full $90 million by 4 million shares gives $22.50, but NAV uses net assets of $80 million, giving $20.

rw: ETFs can be bought and sold at market prices all day on exchanges, whereas mutual funds are priced once per day at the net asset value.

ww.Mutual funds trade all day long on excha: This reverses the facts; ETFs trade throughout the day on exchanges like stocks, while mutual funds are bought or sold at one price after the close.
ww.ETFs trade once per month on the exchang: ETFs trade continuously during market hours, not once per month; a monthly fixed-time trade has no basis in how exchange-traded funds work.
ww.They are identical in every way, includi: ETFs and mutual funds differ in trading: ETFs trade on exchanges all day, while mutual funds are priced once daily, so calling them identical is wrong.

rw: A hedge fund is a private pooled investment that uses varied strategies, such as leverage and short selling, and is generally open to accredited or wealthy investors.

ww.A type of insurance product sold to weal: Insurance is a risk transfer product; a hedge fund is an investment pool that uses varied strategies, usually open only to wealthy or institutional investors.
ww.A public savings account open to anyone: A public savings account open to anyone is a bank product; hedge funds are private, less regulated, and limited to qualified investors.
ww.A bond that pays interest to holders on: A bond pays fixed interest on set dates; a hedge fund is a pooled investment vehicle using flexible strategies rather than a single debt instrument.

rw: A penny stock is a low-priced, speculative share of a small company, often thinly traded and volatile, so investors can lose much of their money.

ww.A blue-chip stock of a large and stable: A blue-chip stock belongs to a large, stable, established company; a penny stock is the opposite, a low-priced, risky share of a small firm.
ww.A high-priced stock trading at a large d: A penny stock has a low price, typically under $5, not a high price; high-priced shares of large firms are not what the term describes.
ww.A government bond issued by the Treasury: Treasury debt is a government bond, not a stock; a penny stock is a share of a small company that trades at a very low price.

rw: An RIA is a firm or individual registered with the SEC or a state to give investment advice for a fee, and owes clients fiduciary duty.

ww.A bank teller who handles deposits and w: A bank teller handles deposits and withdrawals for customers; a registered investment adviser is a firm or person registered to provide investment advice for compensation.
ww.A credit bureau that tracks borrowing hi: A credit bureau tracks borrowing history for lenders; an RIA gives investment advice to clients and is registered with the SEC or a state.
ww.A stock exchange where shares of public: A stock exchange is a marketplace where shares trade; an RIA is a professional adviser to clients, not a place where securities are traded.

rw: A custodian is a financial institution, often a bank or trust company, that holds clients' securities for safekeeping and handles settlement, so assets stay separate from the adviser.

ww.A company's janitor who cleans the offic: A janitor cleans offices; in investing, a custodian is a financial institution that keeps clients' securities safe, so the word has a different meaning here.
ww.A stock picker who selects shares for th: Picking shares for clients is the work of a portfolio manager or adviser; a custodian holds and safeguards the assets but does not choose investments.
ww.A tax agency that collects taxes from fi: Taxes are collected by revenue agencies; a custodian in investing safeguards securities for clients and does not collect taxes from anyone.

rw: A clearinghouse settles trades by confirming details and ensuring buyers and sellers meet their obligations, which reduces the risk that one side defaults on the deal.

ww.A grocery store that sells food and drin: A grocery store sells food; a clearinghouse is a financial institution that stands between buyers and sellers to settle trades and reduce counterparty risk.
ww.A tax office that processes returns for: Tax returns are processed by revenue offices; a clearinghouse handles settlement of securities trades, not taxes for states or the nation.
ww.A company that prints stock certificates: Printing stock certificates is a transfer or printing service; a clearinghouse completes trades by matching, settling, and guaranteeing the obligations of both parties.

rw: T+1 settlement means a trade settles one business day after the trade date, when cash and securities change hands, a standard in U.S. markets.

ww.Settles in one year after the date of th: T+1 means one business day, not one year; a settlement taking a year would make trading impractical, and the T stands for trade date.
ww.Settles instantly on the same day as the: Same-day settlement is called T+0; T+1 means settlement occurs one business day after the trade date, so it is not instant.
ww.Settles in one month after the date of t: One month would be T+30; T+1 adds a single business day to the trade date, which is far shorter than a month.

rw: A conflict of interest arises when an advisor's own interests, such as higher commissions, could compromise advice to a client, so it must be disclosed or avoided.

ww.A type of stock that pays high dividends: A high-dividend stock is an investment type; a conflict of interest is a situation in which an adviser's own interests could compromise advice to clients.
ww.A tax rule that applies to investors who: A tax rule on investors selling at a profit is capital gains tax; a conflict of interest concerns competing interests that can bias advice.
ww.A market holiday when the exchanges are: A market holiday is a day exchanges are closed; a conflict of interest is an ethical issue and has no connection to the exchange calendar.

rw: Suitability requires recommending investments that fit a client's profile and goals, including age, income, risk tolerance, and time horizon, so advice serves the client's needs.

ww.Ignoring client goals when making a reco: Ignoring client goals violates suitability, which requires recommendations to match the client's objectives, risk tolerance, and financial situation, not to disregard them.
ww.Selling the highest-fee product to every: Selling the highest-fee product regardless of fit puts the broker's income ahead of the client, which suitability rules prohibit.
ww.Recommending whatever is popular at the: Recommending what is popular ignores each client's individual needs; suitability requires recommendations tailored to the client's profile, not based on trends.

rw: Know your customer rules require firms to verify identity and understand a client's financial situation, needs, and risk tolerance, which helps prevent fraud and money laundering.

ww.To advertise products and services to th: Advertising is marketing; KYC rules concern verifying clients and understanding their needs, so promotion to the public is unrelated to their purpose.
ww.To list stocks on an exchange for sale t: Listing stocks for sale on an exchange is handled by the exchange and issuer; KYC rules focus on the client relationship, not securities listings.
ww.To raise commissions earned by the broke: KYC rules do not exist to raise commissions; they protect clients and the system by requiring brokers to know who they serve and what they need.

rw: The Series 7 license qualifies a person as a registered representative to sell most securities, including stocks, bonds, and mutual funds, after passing the FINRA exam.

ww.A tax license to prepare returns for cli: Tax preparation licenses are issued by revenue agencies; the Series 7 is a securities license for brokers, not for preparing returns.
ww.A banking license to take deposits and m: A banking license permits taking deposits and lending; the Series 7 is a securities industry qualification and has no role in banking operations.
ww.A real estate license to sell homes and: Real estate sales licenses are issued by states; the Series 7 relates to securities brokerage, so it does not allow selling homes and land.

rw: CFP stands for Certified Financial Planner, a professional credential for people who provide financial planning advice after meeting education, exam, experience, and ethics requirements.

ww.A stock exchange where shares of public: A stock exchange is a marketplace for trading; CFP is a personal credential held by individuals and does not name an exchange.
ww.A tax form filed by investors who own sh: A tax form is a document filed with the IRS; CFP is a professional designation for planners, not a form for owners of shares.
ww.A bank that lends money to firms and to: A bank lends money to firms and homeowners; the CFP is a professional credential for individuals, so it cannot be a lending institution.

rw: CFA stands for Chartered Financial Analyst, a credential for investment professionals earned by passing three exams and meeting work experience requirements.

ww.A bond type that is issued by corporatio: A bond type is a security issued by borrowers; the CFA charter is a professional credential, so it does not describe any security or rating.
ww.A stock index that tracks the largest co: A stock index tracks market performance, whereas the CFA charter is a credential for individual professionals and not a measure of any share prices.
ww.A tax audit that the IRS performs on inv: A tax audit is a government review; the CFA charter is awarded by CFA Institute to people who pass three exams and meet experience rules.

rw: Form ADV is the disclosure document registered investment advisers file with the SEC and provide to clients, describing services, fees, conflicts, and disciplinary history.

ww.A bank statement that lists deposits and: A bank statement lists account activity; Form ADV is a registration document that advisers file with the SEC, covering their business, fees, and conflicts.
ww.A tax return filed by individuals and fi: A tax return reports income to the revenue agency; Form ADV is an adviser disclosure filing and has no role in reporting an individual's taxes.
ww.A loan application filed with a bank for: A loan application is a bank credit form; Form ADV relates to investment adviser registration and disclosure, not borrowing money for cars or houses.

rw: A 22-year-old with a stable job and long horizon can take equity risk, and diversified stock funds provide growth with broad diversification across many companies.

ww.Mostly short-term bonds and cash: Short-term bonds and cash offer safety but low growth, which would waste the long time horizon of a 22-year-old with a stable job.
ww.A single speculative stock held: A single speculative stock concentrates risk in one company, which can fall sharply or fail, so it is not suitable even for a young investor.
ww.All in cash and savings accounts: Cash and savings accounts earn little and may not beat inflation, so holding everything there sacrifices the long-term growth a 22-year-old needs.

rw: A retiree needing steady income and low risk is best served by high-quality bonds and dividend payers, which provide regular income with limited price swings.

ww.Futures speculation for large gains: Futures speculation uses leverage and can produce large losses quickly, so it conflicts with a retiree's need for steady income and low risk.
ww.A single startup firm in the tech sector: A single startup is highly risky and pays no steady income, so it is unsuitable for a 68-year-old who needs stable returns.
ww.Penny stocks of tiny companies abroad: Penny stocks of tiny companies are volatile, thinly traded, and often pay no income, which is unsuitable for a retiree seeking low risk.

rw: If the company struggles, you could lose your job and your savings at once, because both your income and investments depend on the same company.

ww.It always has tax benefits for all the h: Employer stock has no guaranteed tax benefit for all holders, and tax treatment is not the main concern; the real danger is concentrating risk in one company.
ww.Employer stock cannot lose value, so it: Employer stock can lose value, as employees of failed companies learned, so calling it safe is false and holding too much of it is risky.
ww.It is not allowed under the law of the l: Owning employer stock is generally legal; the concern is risk concentration, not a legal ban, so the claim that the law forbids staff from holding it is false.

rw: Systematic risk is market-wide risk from factors such as recessions or interest rates, and it cannot be eliminated by diversification because it affects nearly all assets.

ww.Risk unique to one company, reducible by: Risk unique to one company that diversification can reduce is unsystematic risk; systematic risk affects the entire market and cannot be diversified away.
ww.Risk from fraud committed by the firm's: Fraud by management is a company-specific risk, which is unsystematic and can be reduced through diversification; systematic risk affects the whole market.
ww.Risk from taxes imposed by the governmen: Tax changes can affect certain investors, but systematic risk refers to market-wide forces such as recessions, inflation, and interest rates, not a single tax rule.

rw: Unsystematic risk is specific to one company or industry, such as a product failure or a strike, and holding many different stocks can reduce it.

ww.Interest rate changes that affect all bo: Interest rate changes that affect all bonds are market-wide, which is systematic risk; unsystematic risk is specific to a single company or industry.
ww.Inflation across the whole economy in a: Inflation across the whole economy affects all firms and is systematic risk; unsystematic risk is limited to a particular company or industry.
ww.Market-wide risk that cannot be removed: Market-wide risk that cannot be removed describes systematic risk; unsystematic risk is the opposite, and diversification can reduce it by spreading holdings.
